_comment: SAT-SA operational pattern configuration.
WHAT THIS LAYER IS FOR
A normal SOC dashboard already shows alert counts, severities and open
queues. This layer looks for operational *shape* inside one assessment
scope that a count-based dashboard does not make obvious, and that a
supervisor might reasonably want to look at.
WHAT A SIGNAL IS NOT
A signal here is a request for human review. It is not a finding of
misconduct, not a control failure, and not a risk level. Control
failure language belongs to the execution-gap layer, which is the only
layer whose logic can actually establish a contradicted expectation.
Every status here is therefore qualified as POTENTIAL or reported as
NOT_EVALUABLE.
NO INVENTED THRESHOLDS
Two failure modes are explicitly avoided.
'if count > 10' / 'if share > 0.8'
An asset carrying 60% of a scope's alerts is unremarkable in a
small scope and notable in a large one. A fixed cut-point on a
raw count or share cannot distinguish those cases, so none is
used. Concentration is instead judged against what the scope's
OWN population would produce by chance, which is a property of
the data rather than a number chosen here.
'closure < 5' / 'word_count <= 2'
These legacy rules were deliberately removed from SAT-SA because
they encoded an expectation nobody could justify. They are not
reintroduced, and no pattern below depends on a raw magnitude
cut-point of that kind.
Every number this layer uses is one of exactly three things:
1. a minimum observation count, required by the analytical method and
declared in 'methodology' below so it is visible, not buried;
2. a statistical significance level belonging to the method; or
3. an explicitly configurable parameter, defaulted here and adjustable
by configuration rather than by editing detector code.
Each pattern names the method that produced its number and the
minimum observations that method needs. When a scope holds fewer
observations than the method requires, the pattern returns
NOT_EVALUABLE with an explanation instead of producing a number
that would look precise and mean nothing. There is deliberately no
single global minimum: 'enough observations' depends on the method.

summary: Null hypothesis: the scope's records are distributed across its
observed assets uniformly at random. Under that hypothesis the
count on the busiest asset is Binomial(n, 1/k) for n scope
records and k distinct assets, so the observed count has a
computable probability. The signal is raised only when that
probability is small enough to be unlikely by chance.
This is why no share cut-point is needed: the question asked is
'would this concentration arise by chance in a scope this
size?', not 'is this share above a number someone picked'.
asset_concentration.null_hypothesis: records are distributed uniformly at random across the observed distinct assets
asset_concentration.alternative: one asset carries more records than chance explains
alpha_justification: alpha is a statistical significance level belonging to the test,
not a supervisory policy. 0.01 is a conventional, conservative
level: it means an observed concentration of this kind would
arise by chance in fewer than 1 scope in 100. It does not mean
the asset is risky, and it is configurable rather than fixed.
computation: Computed exactly in-process with integer binomial
coefficients. No model artefact, no training step and no
numerical dependency, so the result is reproducible offline

_comment: Declared here so the requirement is inspectable. A binomial
tail over 4 or 5 records cannot distinguish concentration
from coincidence at any meaningful level, and a single-asset
scope has nothing to be concentrated relative to.

summary: Investigation evidence is reduced to a set of normalised tokens.
Two records are similar when the Jaccard overlap of their token
sets reaches the configured minimum. Records are then grouped
into connected components of mutual similarity, and a component
large enough to be unlikely by chance is reported.
Repetition is reported as a shape across the population, never as
a judgement about any single note. A single terse note is not
evidence of anything; many notes drawn from the same small
vocabulary is a pattern a supervisor may want to understand.
similarity_justification: 0.8 is used as the default because Jaccard is 1.0 only for
identical token sets and falls away quickly as vocabulary
differs, so 0.8 corresponds to near-identical vocabulary rather
than merely topical overlap. It is a configurable parameter, not
a supervisory policy, and it is applied identically to every

_comment: Similarity components are meaningless on a handful of
records: with 4 records almost any pair can be called
similar. The floor also requires several assets to be
involved, because repetition confined to one asset is an
asset pattern rather than an investigation pattern.
Significance level for the concentration test. Statistical, not
policy. Exposed here so it can be changed without touching code.

patterns.name: Alert activity concentrated on a single asset
description: One asset carries a larger share of an assessment scope's alert
records than chance explains for a population of that size.
reason_template: uniform random allocation of {scope_record_count} records across
{distinct_groups} assets, {group_record_count} or more on a single
asset has a probability {probability_phrase}, so this
concentration is unlikely to have arisen by chance.
why_review_might_be_warranted: Repeated activity on one asset may reflect a genuine incident
requiring sustained response, a monitoring or triage path that
funnels work onto a single system, or a recording convention
that attributes work to the asset rather than to the activity.
None of these can be distinguished from the data alone, which
is why this is a request to inspect rather than a conclusion.
explanation_limitations: Concentration establishes distribution, not cause. The pattern
cannot distinguish a persistent campaign, a noisy sensor, and a
systematic triage bias, and it says nothing about whether the

patterns.name: Investigation evidence drawn from a repeated vocabulary
description: A group of investigations in one assessment scope share highly
similar evidence text, indicating they were written from a
repeated vocabulary rather than from record-specific findings.
reason_template: {group_size} investigations in this assessment scope share
near-identical evidence text: the lowest pairwise token overlap
within the group is {observed_min_similarity}, against a configured
assets. Repetition across multiple assets is more consistent with
a templated recording habit than with a single incident.
content_disclosure: The submitted investigation text is never reproduced in a
finding. Only counts, the similarity statistic and record
references are emitted, so an examiner can open the underlying
records under their own access control without this layer
why_review_might_be_warranted: Repeated near-identical investigation text may indicate
templated or copied recording rather than analysis specific to
each case. It may equally reflect a legitimately formulaic
playbook, a copy-paste workflow, or a tooling limitation. The
pattern cannot tell these apart, which is why it asks for a look
explanation_limitations: Token overlap measures wording, not investigative rigour. A
thorough investigation and a superficial one can be equally
repetitive, and a short note can be highly specific. No

unavailable_patterns.name: Unusual closure behaviour
missing_evidence: RESOLUTION_TIME and EVENT_TIMESTAMP both exist as canonical
concepts and can resolve from source columns, so raw timing
evidence is possible in principle.
No authoritative closure expectation exists anywhere in the
repository: no configured SLA, no mandated response window, and
no per-CSE closure objective.
No historical or peer baseline of closure times exists, so a
closure time cannot be called unusual relative to anything.
why_not_implemented: Establishing that a closure is unusual requires a reference to
be unusual against. The legacy 'closure < 5' rule encoded an
expectation nobody could justify and was deliberately removed
from SAT-SA; reintroducing it, in any disguised form, would
restore exactly the unsupported judgement that was deleted.
Producing a signal here would mean the tool inventing its own
notion of a reasonable closure time.
would_require: A configured closure expectation supplied by a supervisory
authority, such as a mandated response window per severity, or
a historical closure baseline per CSE.

unavailable_patterns.name: Multivariate outlier signal
missing_evidence: data/generated/isolation_forest.pkl exists and is a genuine
sklearn.ensemble._iforest.IsolationForest, but scikit-learn is
not importable from the interpreter that runs SAT-SA, so the
model cannot be loaded.
The pickled model expects a 16-dimensional vector
(severity_score, asset_criticality_score, response_time_minutes,
fast_closure, sla_breach, evidence_count, missing_evidence,
missing_root_cause, missing_remediation, missing_escalation,
investigation_quality, low_investigation_quality,
investigation_time_minutes, short_investigation,
note_similarity, template_investigation).
None of these are canonical SAT-SA concepts. They belong to a
different feature pipeline that produces no code in this
repository, and no training population or feature-extraction
path exists that could rebuild that vector.
The companion data/generated/features.csv and
features_anomaly.csv are likewise orphaned artefacts: nothing in
framework/ reads or writes them.
why_not_implemented: Loading a model whose feature contract cannot be reproduced
would produce numbers that cannot be explained or defended, and
an unexplainable anomaly is exactly what this layer exists to
avoid. Hand-rolling a substitute estimator would also mean
building a new ML framework, which is out of scope.
Note also that an Isolation Forest score is a statement about
distance in a feature space, not about supervisory relevance;
even a working model would need an explanation layer before it
could support a reviewable signal.
would_require: scikit-learn available to the SAT-SA runtime, and
A reproducible feature-extraction path mapping canonical
concepts onto the model's expected vector, with a documented
training and inference population, plus a feature-attribution
method able to say which feature drove a score.

unavailable_patterns.name: Operational drift across periods
missing_evidence: This phase evaluates each assessment scope independently and
never pools scopes, so no cross-period comparison exists to
detect drift.
Only two period labels exist in the current fixtures, which is
not a time series.
why_not_implemented: Pooling periods or entities to compare them is explicitly out of
scope for this phase, and an operational pattern that is normal
in one CSE or period may be routine in another. Building the
comparison now would defeat the scope isolation this layer is
required to preserve.
would_require: A deliberate longitudinal analysis phase with an agreed
comparison basis across CSEs or periods.

unavailable_patterns.name: Unusual alert volume
missing_evidence: No expected record volume, no historical baseline, no peer
group and no coverage statement exists for any CSE.
why_not_implemented: A record count is only 'unusual' relative to an expectation. In
the absence of any baseline, every period looks unremarkable and
any threshold applied to a raw count would encode a volume
assumption that SAT-SA has no basis to make.
